2418.idn: inland Leki (as opposed to 'Lakeside Leki' / 'Jita-like Leki'), speakers of Nyang'ombe village, Ukara Island (a named variety of the language); data: fieldwork in Nyang'ombe (Nyango'mbe) village at the centre of Ukara Island, Ukerewe district, Mwanza region, Tanzania; fieldwork date not stated…
2418.tone: Source describes tone only: symbols list (p. viii) has High, Low and Rise-fall tone; sec. 4.3.5 gives H vs L on the verb template distinguishing present retrospective from remote past (Ná-ta-íle vs Nà-ta-ìle), high tone on the progressive marker -e- and on past-habitual pronouns, and concludes that 'tone can be considered as playing grammatical roles'. The word 'stress' occurs once in the whole text and refers to English suffixes ('English non-neutral suffixes which undergo auto-stress (see Katamba, 1993)'); 'accent', 'penult', 'prosod', 'pitch' have no hits. No stress or accent statement for Kara exists in any file held. Caveat: Magesa 2017 (Swahili-language OUT thesis on Kikara tense morphemes, p. 109) asserts in passing that Kikara, like Kiswahili, is among Bantu languages 'ambazo hazina toni' (which have no tone); its Kikara data carry no diacritics and the claim is unsupported, whereas Masatu marks tonal minimal pairs and SIL ESR 2017-002 Appendix I carries acute marks on Nyang'ombe Kara forms; the JE25 cluster (Jita, Downing 1996) is tonal. Tonal reading kept at low confidence.

2419.tone: Lesley-Neuman 2007 sec. 2.3 'Tone' (p. 13): 'Karimojong is a tonal language with a three tone system shown in (13).' -- H (rising-angle diacritic), M (unmarked or level diacritic), L (falling-angle diacritic), plus HL, ML, LM contours; grammatical tone for tense/mood/voice/verb class; all data after Novelli 1985:37 (whose transcriptions she calls 'in need of verification'). 'stress' occurs 0 times in LN2007 (148 pp.) and 0 times in LN2012 (SAL 41). Vossen 1982 sec. 7.2.2.1.3 (Koehler's 200-word list): high, low and high-falling tones marked; nothing on stress. Dimmendaal 2012 cites Novelli 1985:197-497 for the fixed tonal melodies of Karimojong verb morphology. Roncari & Mantovani 1973 never mention tone; their Italian-school 'accento' on a three-tone language is most plausibly the prominent (high-toned) syllable heard as stress, exactly as the catalog already treats Barrett 1988's 'Accent' note for the sister lect Turkana (turk1308: tone or pitch accent, accent note secondary; same EROT/EKILE/ABERU/EKETATAMAN examples from the same Comboni teaching tradition).

tn.quote: Karimojong is a tonal language with a three tone system shown in (13). ... The mid tone is normally written without a diacritic, as shown in (13-b). ... Combination tones, which consist of an unbroken series of two tones over the same vowel, are rarely heard. There is a tendency in the language to drop the second of two tones in a combination (Novelli, 1985), except where there are semantic requirements for its retention. As shown in (15), the attested combination tones are high-low, mid-low, and low-mid.

2420.prule: fixed-final, quantity-insensitive: primary stress on the last syllable of the stem, i.e. the right edge of the phonological word (stem + derivational suffixes, all of which are stressed); enclitics (tense-aspect markers, the indefinite article =dõ/=õ, most postpositions) are unstressed and do not alter the stem's stress.
2420.srule: Secondary stress on every other syllable counting leftward from the stem-final primary stress (iambic, right-to-left): wa-riOrE [waˌriOˈrE] 'my child', wa-riOrE-riOrE [ˌwariˌoreˌriOˈrE] 'my grandchild'; the pattern is recomputed over compounds and derived (suffixed) words.

2421.prule: No general word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the sketch (the Phonology section, pp.444-446, has no stress paragraph). Stress is given morpheme by morpheme: the case/number suffixes -ə (obl.sg., dir.pl.) and -un/-on (obl.pl.) are stressed; the attributive linker -e is unstressed and the stress falls on the following noun; the disyllabic personal pronouns ave, ame, šeme and the demonstrative/personal pronouns are stressed on the last syllable; the negative copula carries the stress on the prefix ni- (nine, niše, nie, nimbe, ninie, ninde); the preterit of 'to be' (bine, biše, bie, bimbe, binye, binde) is stressed on the first syllable; the imperfect/infinitive formant -e and the perfect marker -ā added to stem II are stressed. Kalasuri (Yarshater 2005) matches: stressed -e/-i/-un case suffixes, unstressed adjectival linker, stressed tense formants -e/-a, and an unstressed preterit marker -i- 'with the stress falling on the last syllable of the stem'. Inference only (not the author's rule): every nominal statement is consistent with word-final stress (stressed inflectional suffixes, end-stressed pronouns, unstressed ezafe-like linker), the usual Persian/Tatic pattern; verb forms instead stress the tense formant, the negative prefix or the first syllable (Karingani níne, bíne; Kalasuri preterit genést-i-m), so the final-stress reading holds for nominals only.

2422.prule: No stress rule stated. Karko is presented as a tone language: every example carries high, mid or low tone marks or a falling/rising contour; tone is 'a property of a syllable', not of a vowel; contour tones arise when the tone of a lost syllabic suffix attaches to the root; singular and plural 'can even be solely marked by tonal contrast'. The words stress/accent occur in the article only in 'tonal accents' (= tone diacritics). No word-stress position is given anywhere.

Garko' = Karko per Glottolog alt name; 1914 data, consulted again:): 'Die Beobachtung des Stärkeakzents ist außerordentlich erschwert durch die scheinbar willkürliche Behandlung desselben.'... 'Ich habe den Eindruck, als wenn zwar musikalische Töne vorliegen, als ob sie aber durch die Stellung im Satz sich ändern, so daß ihre sichere Ermittelung erschwert wird.' = stress accent could not be pinned down; musical tones (Klingenheben: Hochton/Mittelton/Tiefton) seem present but shift with sentence position. 2423.dq: Toutefois, la hauteur musicale et l’accent dynamique sont prévisibles dans le mot phonologique, selon les règles suivantes. (§3.4 is headed 'Le mot phonologique'; §3.4.2 states that vowel harmony spreads over all vowels of a word and never beyond word boundaries, the same domain.)
2423.dloc: §3.4.3 'La hauteur musicale et l’accent dynamique' with §3.4.3.1 'La hauteur musicale' and §3.4.3.2 'L’accent dynamique', document pp. 15-17; §3.2.1.2 'Les consonnes longues', doc pp. 10-11 (the remark itself on doc p. 11), for the consonant-length remark.
2423.heavy: 'syllabes lourdes, c’est-à-dire du type (C)VV, (C)VVC ou CVNC' (long vowel, long vowel + coda, or short vowel + nasal-plus-consonant coda) = heavy; 'Une syllabe fermée, c’est-à-dire du type (C)VC' = intermediate, accented only when no heavy is present; 'syllabes légères, c’est-à-dire du type (C)V' = light. Note that CVNC (short vowel + NC cluster) is ranked with the long-vowel syllables above plain CVC.
2423.dflt: If no heavy but a closed (C)VC syllable: the closed syllable(s). If all syllables are light: the first syllable ([ˈcɐpɐ], [ˈɛjɐnʊ]), plus the penult when the word has more than three syllables ([ˈɛpʊlɐˈpʊlɐ]).
2423.prule: Word-level 'accent dynamique' (intensity stress) assigned by a three-tier syllable-weight scale, unbounded, stated with hedges ('Il semble', 'semblent diriger'): (a) every heavy syllable — (C)VV, (C)VVC or CVNC — carries the accent (in the rare words with three heavies, the first and last are accented and the middle one weakened); (b) if there is no heavy syllable, a closed (C)VC syllable carries it (both, if there are two: [ˈcɛmˈmɛk], [kɐˈfɔŋkɔˈlɔŋ]); (c) if all syllables are light (C)V, the first syllable is accented, and in words of more than three syllables the penult is accented as well ([ˈɛpʊlɐˈpʊlɐ] 'canard'). At most two accents per word, of about the same intensity. Examples: [ˈkɐːwɐk] 'creuser', [ɐˈɲɪː] 'enfant', [kɐˈsɐːˈlɐːt], [cikiˈsoːl] 'laboure!', [ˈkɐːpʊɲɐˈnɔːl], [ɛlɐˈwʊt], [ˈkɐːkɔsʊˈkɔs], [ˈcɐpɐ] 'oignon', [ˈɛjɐnʊ]. Independently, a fixed pitch peak ('hauteur musicale', 'un ton plus haut') sits on the penultimate syllable of every phonological word (schemas for 2-, 3-, 4-syllable words).
2423.srule: No primary/secondary ranking: a word carries at most two 'accents dynamiques' of roughly equal intensity ('un mot porte au maximum deux accents dynamiques, qui ont à peu près la même intensité'). A second accent falls on a second heavy syllable ([kɐˈsɐːˈlɐːt]; with three heavies, first and last accented, middle weakened), on a second closed syllable when there is no heavy ([ˈcɛmˈmɛk], [kɐˈfɔŋkɔˈlɔŋ]), and in all-light words of more than three syllables on the penult, the syllable bearing the pitch peak ([ˈɛpʊlɐˈpʊlɐ]); no word, even five-syllable compounds/reduplications, showed more than two.

2430.qtr: Stress in Kaxarari cannot, therefore, be considered predictable; it is more adequate to postulate that there are two distinct groups of words with respect to stress, in one group the words bearing stress on the last syllable and in a second set the words bearing their stress on the penultimate syllable. Thus the question of stress in Kaxarari remains open for further study. Another point that can be raised is that no occurrence of stress on the antepenultimate syllable was found in the corpus, so there appear to be no constructions of the type #'CV.CV.CV#.
2430.dq: Sousa 2004 p. 79: 'há dois grupos distintos de palavras quanto ao acento, sendo que em um grupo as palavras portam o acento na última sílaba, e em um segundo conjunto, as palavras portam o respectivo acento na penúltima sílaba' (all examples are single words in citation form). Couto 2005 sec. 11.3 contrasts word and phrase explicitly: 'A pronúncia da palavra isolada tem uma entonação diferente da…
2430.dloc: Sousa 2004, Cap. III sec. 3.4 'Acento', p. 79. Couto 2005, sec. 11.3 'Acentuação e Tom', p. 26.
2430.prule: Lexically specified: Kaxarari words fall into two lexical classes, one stressed on the final syllable (/pu'nu/ 'veia', /kala'ka/ 'trovão', /tamapa'ʃa/ 'castanha do pará', /i'pa/ 'pai', /ika'ni/ 'frio'), the other on the penult (/'maβi/ 'barro, terra', /'kili/ 'buraco', /ti'tiʃi/ 'carvão', /'uʃi/ 'lua', /u'hila/ 'vento'); stress 'não pode ser... considerado previsível'. No antepenultimate stress found in the corpus (two-syllable window at the right edge). Couto 2005 independently gives final stress as the most common/'previsível' pattern in di- and trisyllables but lists eight stress minimal pairs ([a'wa] 'papagaio' vs ['awa] 'besouro', [wa'ka] 'água' vs ['waka] 'timbó', [wa'hi] 'chuva' vs ['wahi] 'roçado'...), so both first-hand descriptions agree that stress is contrastive.

Assim, a questão do acento em Kaxarari fica em aberto para maiores estudos. tn.quote: Há a presença de dois tons em Kaxarari, um alto e um baixo, que aparentemente não carregam muita carga semântica. De fato, o tom alto parece acompanhar a sílaba tônica. A pronúncia da palavra isolada tem uma entonação diferente da palavra numa frase, onde a prosódia do grupo rítmico parece determinar o padrão de acentuação de cada vocábulo. Em relação às palavras isoladas, há pares mínimos demonstrando contraste de intensidade, alterando seus significados. ... Igualmente, estudos futuros serão precisos em relação aos tons.
tn.translation: Two tones are present in Kaxarari, a high one and a low one, which apparently do not carry much semantic load. In fact, the high tone seems to accompany the stressed syllable. The pronunciation of the word in isolation has a different intonation from the word in a sentence, where the prosody of the rhythmic group seems to determine the accentuation pattern of each word. As regards isolated words, there are minimal pairs showing a contrast of intensity, changing their meanings. ... Likewise, future studies will be needed regarding the tones.

2431.heavy: none: no syllable-weight criterion is mentioned anywhere; the positions given are by syllable count only. Fn.10 (p.8) says long vowels occur only in slow speech in CV syllables ([mah'ta.tsi] 'worm', [ki'tsa.re] 'manioc', [ma'ri.yo] 'knife'), a consequence of slow speech, not a condition on accent placement.
2431.dflt: not applicable (no weight criterion; the classification "lexical"). Where the source gives a position it is the 2nd syllable from the left (final in disyllables).
2431.prule: The author's own analysis is that the primary accent is phonemic (contrastive): 'Cada palavra é caracterizada pelo acento primário, fonêmico conforme atestam os seguintes pares mínimos: /'akoro/ = contigo, /a'koro/ = com êle, /'akoro?ne/ = com vocês, /a'koro?ne/ = com êles' (p.16), restated in the English summary 'Word stress is phonemic although it can be predicted in some environments' (p.20). The predictable environments she gives are quantity-insensitive and put the primary accent on the second syllable from the left: disyllables 'geralmente' take it on the last (= 2nd) syllable (/to'ho/, /ka'mi/, /a'koy/, /we'we/; isolation-form exceptions /'kwama/, /'papa/, which take final accent inside a pause group); 4-syllable words have the primary on the 2nd with a non-phonemic secondary on the 4th ([ta'rako'ro], [ku'rata'ku]); the six trisyllabic examples (p.17: /a'sakre/, /a'ware/, /ka'yahi/, /tak'pire/, /kah'rutu/, /ka'myere/) and six quadrisyllabic examples (p.18: /weh'tohoro/, /o'nemawi/, /a'imunu/, /pri'prikono/, /a'kantaki/, /kwa'sikana/) are all marked on the 2nd, but no prose rule is given for trisyllables; 5-syllable words carry accents on the 2nd and 5th ([a'marisi'pa], [a'kayahi'ni]) 'havendo portanto um espaço de duas sílabas entre os acentos secundário e primário', which does not say unambiguously which of the two is primary (the same tick marks both). Dominant position in the data: 2nd syllable from the left (final in disyllables); the source states no single fixed position across word lengths and expressly labels the accent phonemic. Live alternative reading: fixed and quantity-insensitive, 2nd syllable, grid '01 010 0100', which a fuller source (Paula 1980) could confirm or refute.
2431.srule: Non-phonemic secondary accent, hedged ('pode haver'), in words of 4+ syllables: 4-syllable words primary on the 2nd, secondary on the 4th (final) syllable ([ta'rako'ro] 'all', [ku'rata'ku] 'grasshopper'); 5-syllable words accents on the 2nd and 5th (final) 'with a space of two syllables between the secondary and primary accents' ([a'marisi'pa], [a'kayahi'ni]) — the same tick marks both, so which of 2nd/5th is primary is not stated. Words of 1-3 syllables: one accent only.

2433.heavy: A syllable with an onset consonant ('the first consonant-initial syllable', 'the first syllable with an onset', 'the first vowel preceded by a consonant'); an onsetless word-initial syllable is skipped. Additionally, a word-initial long vowel /ɐː/ attracts stress (stated as the single exception to the onset rule).
2433.dflt: Not stated as such; the rule presupposes a consonant in the root (every root has one; minimal roots like ake [ɐˈkɐ] 'head' stress the final post-consonantal vowel). No all-vowel words are discussed.
2433.prule: One stress per prosodic word (= root or polysyllabic affix), on the first syllable that has an onset consonant: consonant-initial words are stressed on the initial syllable (kayte [ˈkai.tə] 'grub', taltye [ˈtal.cə] 'raindrop'), vowel-initial words on the second syllable (aleke [aˈlə.kə] 'dog', artetye [a.ˈʈə.cə] 'mulga'). The position is therefore sigma1 or sigma2 from the left edge, decided by the presence of an onset in sigma1, not by syllable count. Stated exception: roots with an initial long vowel /ɐː/ stress that initial vowel (aherre [ˈaː.rə] 'kangaroo'). A final vowel is stressed when it is the first post-consonantal vowel of the root (ake [ɐˈkɐ] 'head').
2433.srule: None within the stress domain (prosodic word): 'one stress is assigned for each prosodic word'; 'there is no evidence for secondary stress on monomorphemic roots.
